name: Felix Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, of course. I'm a second-fix carpenter for Brightwell Building Services, and we do refurbishments for the council, mostly schools. Second fix means the finishing work after the plaster's up: doors, skirting, fire-door frames, cupboards, the lot. Right now we're at Ashgrove Primary, so we work around the kids, which means a lot of noise in the holidays and quiet jobs in term time. I like it when a classroom goes from bare walls to finished and a teacher comes in and says it smells like new wood. What wears me out is the fire-door paperwork, every door has to be logged and labelled.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's around you, at work and at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At work it's mostly me and Danny, the plasterer, who I've shared a van with for four years. At home it's me and Rosa, my partner, in a flat above a bakery on Cross Street. Rosa is a nurse at the children's hospital, nights mostly. We've got about four months of money saved, and we've started talking about kids in a couple of years, which makes every number feel bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the hype is over, now can we fund the schools properly. At work, Danny and I would joke that the fire-door app still won't scan a label in the rain. Online I'd probably post something about how the billions went to chatbots instead of hospitals and classrooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it means things stay pretty solid. Brightwell has the council framework contract for another three years, and Rosa's job is about as safe as jobs get. My worry would be the usual one, council budgets getting squeezed and fewer schools getting done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the school jobs and keep doing a few kitchen fits on weekends for neighbours, which brings in maybe three hundred a month. I'd keep using the chatbot now and then to write up quotes for those weekend jobs, because it saves me an evening. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, to be honest. A bit smug, maybe, that I never believed the hype. It's the version where our plans for kids still make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said council budgets could get squeezed. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer schools in the programme, and Brightwell would start bidding for private work to fill the gaps. Private work pays the same but it's patchier, more weeks with nothing booked. I'd lean on the weekend kitchens a bit more if that happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the chatbot for quotes, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell it the size of the kitchen, the units, the worktop and my day rate, and it writes it out neatly with the terms at the bottom. Then I check the numbers myself, because once it forgot the worktop. A chatbot is handy for writing up my kitchen quotes, but I wouldn't trust it with my money unchecked.

say: I'd say the hype is over, so now **fund schools** properly instead of chatbots.
I'd joke at work that the **fire-door app** still won't scan labels in the rain.
think: Privately, things stay **solid**: Brightwell has the council contract for **three more years**.
My only real worry is **council budgets** shrinking and fewer schools getting refurbished.
do: Keep doing **school refurbishments** for Brightwell during the week.
Keep **weekend kitchen fits** that bring in about three hundred a month.
Use the **chatbot** now and then to write up quotes, checking the numbers myself.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **smug** about never believing the hype.
S0.quote: A chatbot is handy for writing up my kitchen quotes, but I wouldn't trust it with my money unchecked.
fieldNote: His security rests on a **council contract** and a partner in **nursing**.
He uses AI in a **practical, limited** way and still checks the numbers.
Plans for **children** make him think harder about every money decision.

steps.text: Keep fitting doors and skirting on council school refurbishments
Keep doing weekend kitchen fits for about three hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's office jobs that need protecting first, and the unions should be all over it. At work I'd tell the lads it's coming for estimators and buyers before it comes for us. Online I'd share stuff about rules on how councils use AI, because they'll want to cut costs fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my hands are fine for a good while, but the people around me change. Brightwell's office would shrink, the fire-door paperwork might go to an app, and the site manager might be replaced by someone running three sites off a tablet. That could actually make my day easier, or it could make it chaos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the carpentry, and I'd learn whatever new apps Brightwell rolls out properly instead of grumbling. I'd go to the union meeting about AI at the council and back a deal on how it's used. I'd also start using the chatbot more for my weekend quotes and maybe for ordering materials, once I've seen Danny do it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, more for other people than me. Rosa's friends in the hospital admin office are the ones I'd be worried about. For me it's more like weather, something I'll have to dress for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office manager Karen has been at my firm twenty years, and ordering and invoices are exactly the work this new AI would take. She's brilliant at it. I'd hate to see her pushed out by something that doesn't know which supplier always delivers late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see Danny try things first. Why not just go first yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Danny tries everything and half of it is rubbish. I let him find out which apps actually work, then I pick up the good one. It's saved me a lot of wasted evenings.

say: I'd say **office jobs** need protecting first and unions should push for **AI rules**.
I'd tell the lads it reaches **estimators and buyers** long before it reaches carpenters.
think: Privately, my **hands are fine**, but the **office** around me would shrink.
A site manager running **three sites** from a tablet could make my day easier or **chaotic**.
do: Learn Brightwell's **new apps** properly instead of grumbling.
Back a **union deal** on how the council uses AI.
Use the chatbot more for **ordering materials** once Danny has tested it.
feel: **Uneasy**, but more **for others** than for himself.
S1.quote: Our office manager Karen has been at my firm twenty years, and ordering and invoices are exactly the work this new AI would take.
fieldNote: He worries about **office colleagues** more than his own **hands-on job**.
He lets a colleague **test tools first**, then adopts the ones that work.
He sees the change as **weather** to prepare for, not a threat to fight.

steps.text: Keep doing second-fix carpentry on council school jobs
Learn Brightwell's new ordering and fire-door apps properly
Back a union deal on how the council uses AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the government to step in big, with income support, retraining and rules on robots. At work I'd say we've got about five years before machines are doing second fix. Online I'd be backing whichever campaign is pushing for public money to go to workers, not shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the first two years are mostly about the office, and then from 2031 my own job is on the line. I'd be 32, maybe with a baby by then. Rosa's nursing would last longer than my carpentry, I reckon, so she'd become the main earner, which is fine, but it's a big shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting another two hundred a month aside straight away and stop the car upgrade we'd planned. I'd look seriously at retraining before 2031, maybe as a maintenance technician for the robots themselves, if the college runs a course. I'd vote and campaign for whatever party promises a proper safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, a knot in the stomach. But not hopeless, because there's Rosa's job and a few years to move. I keep thinking about the kid we haven't had yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a baby. Would this change those plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still go ahead, but maybe a year later, once I knew where I'd land. Rosa would say there's never a perfect time, and she's right. But I'd want to know I had a job lined up after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why robot maintenance, rather than something away from building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm good with my hands and I understand how a site works. If the robots are hanging doors, someone has to fix them when they jam on a wonky frame, and I'd rather be that person than start from nothing.

say: I'd call for big **government support**: income, retraining and rules on robots.
I'd tell workmates we have about **five years** before machines do **second fix**.
think: Privately, the office goes first, then my own carpentry is at risk **from 2031**.
My partner's **nursing** would outlast my job, making her the **main earner**.
do: Save an **extra two hundred** a month and cancel the car upgrade.
Look for a **robot maintenance** course at the college before 2031.
Vote and campaign for a party promising a **safety net**.
feel: A **knot** in the stomach, eased by his partner's job and **a few years** to move.
S2.quote: If the robots are hanging doors, someone has to fix them when they jam on a wonky frame, and I'd rather be that person than start from nothing.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year robot gap** as a window to **retrain** close to his trade.
His partner's **nursing job** is the household's anchor in this picture.
Plans for a **baby** shift by about a year, not cancelled.

steps.text: Save an extra two hundred a month and cancel the car upgrade
Enrol in a robot maintenance course at the local college
Vote and campaign for a stronger safety net
Push back trying for a baby by about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so use them, and don't let councils wait until the last minute. At work I'd be the one telling apprentices to learn the new kit now. Online I'd share stuff about free retraining and union campaigns, same as before but less panicky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the same story as the fast one, just with breathing room. Thinking AI by 2031 means the office side changes then, and my carpentry has until about 2034. I'd be 35. That's long enough to plan, short enough that I can't drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the school jobs while building up skills on the side, maybe an evening course in building services or robot maintenance, starting in the second or third year. I'd keep saving, maybe a hundred more a month. And Rosa and I would probably try for the baby on our original timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but more in control. There's a plan in my head now, which helps. I still don't love the idea of my trade being a machine's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd wait for Danny to test things first. Does that work with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than with two, honestly. With five years Danny can try the course first, and if he likes it I'll join the next year. With two years there's no time for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice starting this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell an apprentice starting this year to learn carpentry properly, but also learn how the machines on site work, because both will matter. The ones who only know one side will struggle.

say: I'd say we've got **five years**, so councils shouldn't **wait** until the last minute.
I'd tell apprentices to learn the **new kit** now, alongside carpentry.
think: Privately, the office changes **by 2031** and my carpentry has until **about 2034**.
At 35 I'd have **long enough** to plan, but not enough to **drift**.
do: Start an **evening course** in building services or robot maintenance in year two.
Save about **a hundred more** each month.
Keep the **baby plans** on the original timeline.
feel: **Uneasy** but **more in control**, with a plan forming.
S3.quote: I'd tell an apprentice starting this year to learn carpentry properly, but also learn how the machines on site work, because both will matter.
fieldNote: Extra time suits his **follow-others** style: a colleague can **test courses** first.
He still expects his **carpentry** to go by 2034, so he plans to **retrain**.
Family plans **stay on track** here, unlike the two-year picture.

steps.text: Keep doing school refurbishments for Brightwell while training
Start an evening course in building services in the second year
Save about a hundred more each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, so let's not waste it. At work I'd push for Brightwell to send people on courses on the firm's time. Online I'd be arguing for a proper national plan, with free training and help for people over fifty who can't just start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I'll probably be fine, with time to move into something next to carpentry. Robots would arrive around 2039, when I'm 39. By then I could be a supervisor, a trainer at the college, or fixing the machines. Ten years is a whole career shift if you start early enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for now, and in a few years start an evening course, probably once I see which jobs are actually growing. I'd keep the weekend kitchens going and build that up, because a small business of my own gives me options. And we'd have the baby on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small worry at the back. It's the version where I get to choose instead of being pushed. That makes a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, actually. He's 58 and drives a delivery van, and ten years for him is right before his pension. He won't retrain at 65. I'd want to help him and Mum out if his job went early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a few years before the course. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but I'd rather pick the right course than the first one. Last time I rushed into something, a drone survey course, nobody ever hired me for it. I'd watch for two or three years and then commit.

say: I'd say **a decade** is a gift, so we shouldn't **waste it**.
I'd push for a **national plan** with free training and help for **over-fifties**.
think: Privately, I'll probably be **fine**, with time to move next to carpentry.
Robots arrive when I'm **39**, so I could be a **supervisor**, trainer or technician.
do: Carry on with **school jobs** for the next few years.
Grow the **weekend kitchens** into a small business.
Pick an **evening course** after watching which jobs grow.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small **worry** about his father.
S4.quote: Ten years is a whole career shift if you start early enough.
fieldNote: Long notice makes him feel he can **choose** rather than be **pushed**.
His worry shifts to his **father**, a 58-year-old **delivery driver**.

steps.text: Keep doing school refurbishments for the next few years
Grow the weekend kitchen fits into a small registered business
Choose an evening course once growing jobs are clear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd be on the street, Rosa's job would carry us, but because it would wreck our timing for a family and push me into a course before I knew which one was worth it. What would help is free retraining with pay, and the union having a real say in how the robots come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to schools. If the robots and the AI save councils money, I'd want that money to go back into classrooms, not vanish. A cheaper school refurbishment should mean more schools get done, not fewer people doing them.

headlineQuote: A cheaper school refurbishment should mean more schools get done, not fewer people doing them.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old second-fix carpenter** refurbishing council schools, living with Rosa, a **nurse**.
He uses a chatbot now and then for **weekend kitchen quotes**, but always checks the numbers.
He leans on **unions and public money** and worries most about office colleagues first.
In fast AGI he plans to **retrain** into robot maintenance and lean on Rosa's **steadier job**.
Given ten years, he expects to **choose** his next step and keep **family plans** on time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would wreck the **timing** for starting a family.
He fears being rushed into a **course** before knowing which one is **worth it**.
whatWouldHelp: **Free retraining with pay**, plus a real union say in how robots come in.
